extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, playwrights, novelists, and other narrative writers seeking craft guidance
extracted.subtask_short: designing acts and conflict in stories
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on structuring narrative through conflict, act design, turning points, and subplot relationships for film, play, and long-form fiction. Emphasizes how to hook and hold audience interest via temporal pacing and layered antagonism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: The music of story is conflict; conflict hooks and holds the audience’s interest and carries them through time without an awareness of its passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict is the temporal engine of narrative—when conflict disappears the audience’s attention leaves. Treat conflict as the soul of story; design the work so conflict continually engages thought and emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict must be meaningful and honestly expressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid either an excess of meaningless, absurdly violent conflict or a vacancy of meaningful conflict; both extremes cause failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: 'turbo special effects' conflict devised by writers insensitive to honest struggles (phony, overwrought mayhem); reactionary avoidance producing low-key depictions that bore. Aim for conflict rooted in genuine human lack or desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three levels of antagonism
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict arises on three levels—inner (mind/soul), personal (relationships), and extra-personal (society/world).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these as distinct sources of antagonism. Examples: inner conflicts (stream of consciousness), personal conflicts (soap opera/domestic drama), extra-personal conflicts (action/adventure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication vs. Complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Complication = conflict concentrated on only one level; Complexity = conflict present on all three levels, often simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complicated works tend to require large casts and multiple locations. To achieve richness, aim for complexity (inner + personal + extra-personal), but keep the overall telling 'relatively simple' in cast and locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not proliferate characters or locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Design relatively simple but complex stories: restrain the number of characters and locations while deepening conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than hopping through time, space, and people, discipline yourself to a reasonably contained cast and world to concentrate on layered conflict. Anti-patterns: 'cast of thousands' and constant location changes that dilute focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beats, scenes, sequences, turning points hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Beats (changing human behavior) build scenes; scenes should ideally be Turning Points where value-charges swing; sequences are series of scenes; sequences build acts culminating in major reversals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every scene becoming a Turning Point creates forward motion; structure sequences to culminate in scenes of moderate impact, and acts to climax in major reversals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-act minimum for full-length narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: For feature-length works (film, full-length play, novel) three major reversals (acts) is the necessary minimum to reach the limits of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One- or two-act designs suit short forms (short story, one-act play, short film). Three acts allow sufficient depth; more acts are possible but bring trade-offs (see multiplicity of acts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Act proportions and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical feature rhythm: Act One ≈ 25% (Act One Climax ~20–30 minutes), Act Two significantly longer, Act Three shortest (ideally <20 minutes) to create acceleration toward the Climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long second acts often bog down; ensure final act is brief to preserve rising acceleration. Use these as approximations, not rigid formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing the long second act
rubrics_metrics.description: If the second act lags, solve it by adding subplots or increasing the number of acts (e.g., Mid-Act Climax to split Act Two into more movements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options: weave subplots with their own act structures to provide additional major reversals between the central plot’s climaxes; or insert Mid-Act Climaxes to create a four- or more-act rhythm. Beware of the costs of adding acts (see clichés/repetition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident placement and setup subplots
rubrics_metrics.description: The Central Plot’s Inciting Incident typically occurs early but can arrive late; when delayed, a setup subplot may be required to engage the audience and reveal the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay the Inciting Incident only for audience-necessary reasons (to know the protagonist). If delayed, use setup subplots to carry interest. If no subplot, use dramatized exposition to hold attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four memorable scenes in a three-act story
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-act story generally requires four powerful turning-point scenes: the Inciting Incident, Act One Climax, Act Two (Penultimate) Climax, and Act Three (Story) Climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These key reversals should be spanned with excellent scenes and sequences to achieve major emotional impact (example: Kramer vs. Kramer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid multiplying act climaxes excessively
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplying acts to force frequent major reversals invites clichés and repetitiousness and reduces the impact of individual climaxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you add many acts (5–8), inventing a major reversal every 15–20 minutes strains creativity and risks making 'major' turns feel routine. Use multi-act designs judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: False Ending usage
rubrics_metrics.description: False Endings are scenes that seem to end the story but do not; they can be effective (Hitchcock examples) but are usually inappropriate for most films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If used, place deliberately for shock or thematic purpose. Generally, the Penultimate Act Climax should intensify the Major Dramatic Question and lead naturally to the Story Climax rather than create a deceptive closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act Rhythm: opposing emotional charges for penultimate and final climaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The two most powerful scenes—the Penultimate and Ultimate (Story) Climax—must not repeat the same emotional charge; they should contradict (one positive, one negative) to preserve impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition halves the power of the second event. If the Story Climax is ironic (mixed charge), determine its overall leaning and design the Penultimate Climax to contradict that leaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot relationships to the Central Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot may (1) contradict the Controlling Idea (irony), (2) resonate the Controlling Idea (variation), (3) serve as a setup when the Central Plot’s Inciting Incident is delayed, or (4) complicate the Central Plot by adding antagonism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subplots intentionally according to these four relationships. Examples: contradiction adds ironic complexity; resonance strengthens theme through variation; complication increases stakes and difficulty for the protagonist; setup holds interest until central action begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and emphasis between Central Plot and subplot
rubrics_metrics.description: Control the balance of screen-time and empathy; deemphasize subplots that distract from the Central Plot, or promote a subplot to Central Plot if it demands greater focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To deemphasize, keep subplot elements (Inciting Incident, climaxes, Crisis, Resolution) offscreen or reduced. Beware: a setup subplot can mislead audience about genre if handled poorly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplot cohesion requires an organizing idea or motif
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplot films without a Central Plot must be held together by an idea, theme, or recurring motif rather than a single plot spine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thematic contradiction and variation to create a portrait (e.g., social landscape). Without a unifying idea, multiplots risk fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot must be thematically or structurally related
rubrics_metrics.description: If a subplot neither contradicts/resonates the Controlling Idea nor sets up or complicates the Central Plot, it will split the story and destroy unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience expects aesthetic unity; every element must relate structurally or thematically. If the relation is absent or unclear, the audience will disengage or attempt to force unity unsuccessfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics (anti-patterns) of single-level 'complicated' stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories complicated on only one level typically show two hallmarks: a large cast and multiple sets/locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize these as indicators: action/adventure often focuses extra-personal conflict with many characters and locations; soap opera focuses personal conflict with many interpersonal sets; stream-of-consciousness focuses inner conflict with dense imagery and many mental 'locations'—all are 'merely complicated' if only one level is used.
